## A Date That Mostly Isn't There

**February 29, 1960.**

Consider what it means to have a birthday that the calendar withholds in three out of every four years. Most people's birthdays are simply there, reliably, every February or June or October. Yours appears and disappears. For 66 years of life, February 29 has arrived sixteen times. On the other fifty years, the date skipped from the 28th to the 1st without acknowledgment — your actual birthday excised from the calendar as if by editorial decision. The next February 29 arrives in 2028, when you'll be 68. There is a particular relationship with time that only leap-day people know: the sense that the ordinary human system for measuring the years doesn't quite have a place for you, and never has.

The day itself, when it comes, carries weight.

---

**The Olympics had closed the day before.**

The VIII Winter Olympic Games had been held at Squaw Valley, California — the first Winter Olympics on American soil — and the closing ceremony took place on February 28, 1960, the day before you were born. America had done well: gold medals in speed skating, figure skating, ice hockey. The games had been unusually intimate, hosted in a valley that barely existed as a resort when the bid was won, built almost from scratch for the occasion. They were also the first Winter Olympics to be televised extensively — CBS broadcast the events, and the technology of sports broadcasting was being invented in real time. You were born the morning after the flame went out.

---

**The ground had moved, eleven thousand miles away.**

On February 29, 1960 — the night before in Moroccan time, the same calendar day — a catastrophic earthquake struck Agadir, a coastal city on the Atlantic. It hit close to midnight. In fifteen seconds, a third of the city's population was dead — between twelve and fifteen thousand people, killed in their sleep. The quake lasted less time than it takes to read this sentence. Agadir had to be rebuilt almost entirely from nothing, and the reconstruction became one of the first large-scale applications of earthquake-resistant urban planning in the developing world. You were born on the same day that a city was destroyed and had to be reimagined.

---

**±30 Days — France Joins the Nuclear Club**

*Sixteen days before you were born*, on February 13, 1960, France detonated its first nuclear device in the Sahara Desert — a test called Gerboise Bleue, Blue Jerboa, after the small desert rodent. The explosion yielded roughly four times the power of the bomb dropped on Hiroshima. France became the fourth nation to possess nuclear weapons, after the United States, the Soviet Union, and Britain. President Charles de Gaulle called it a source of national pride. Algerian independence activists, whose country's soil had just been used as a test site without their consent, drew different conclusions. The Gerboise Bleue test was a milestone in the proliferation that had been making the world more dangerous since 1945 — each new country joining the nuclear club expanding the number of ways the world could end. You were born into a world in which four nations had the capacity to destroy cities from the air with a single device, and that number was climbing.

---

**Cuba was already in motion.**

Fidel Castro had taken power in Havana on January 1, 1959 — fourteen months before you were born. By February 1960, the question of what Cuba would become was already being answered: Castro had signed a trade agreement with the Soviet Union the week before your birthday, and the Eisenhower administration was moving toward the covert plan that would become the Bay of Pigs invasion. The Cuban Revolution, the Bay of Pigs failure, and the Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 all unfolded in the first two and a half years of your life. You were too young to remember any of it consciously. But the Missile Crisis — the thirteen days in October 1962 when the world came closest to nuclear exchange — happened when you were two years old, and the adults around you were afraid in ways that children absorb through the atmosphere of a household even when no one explains what's happening.

---

**Your generation came of age after the illusions broke.**

You were twelve when the last American troops withdrew from Vietnam. Fourteen when Nixon resigned. Sixteen when the United States celebrated its bicentennial in a mood of exhausted ambivalence — a country that had fought a war it couldn't win, suffered an assassination that still hadn't been explained to everyone's satisfaction, and watched its president leave office in disgrace. The political disillusionment that defined the 1970s was the climate of your adolescence. You didn't get to grow up believing the government was honest, because by the time you were old enough to form political opinions, Watergate had happened.

---

**The 1980s arrived with your adulthood.**

You were twenty when Ronald Reagan was elected in November 1980. The decade of your twenties was Reagan's America: the Cold War intensifying before it collapsed, the AIDS epidemic arriving without warning and killing a generation of young people while the government was slow to respond, personal computers moving from hobbyist machines to office necessities to household objects. You were in your twenties during the AIDS crisis — old enough to know people affected, young enough that it was your peers dying. The epidemic that killed more than 700,000 Americans arrived in the first years of your working life and reshaped what it meant to be young in that decade.

---

**The synthesis.**

You have had sixteen February 29 birthdays in 66 years. The seventeenth comes in 2028. Between any two of those real birthdays — four years, 1,461 days — the world has never failed to rearrange itself in some significant way. The leap day keeps returning to find a different planet. In 1964 you were four, Kennedy had just been shot, the Civil Rights Act was being debated. In 1984 you were twenty-four, the Cold War was still permanent-seeming, and a computer that fit on a desk was a remarkable object. In 2024 you were sixty-four, and a machine could write poetry and hold a conversation. The four-year intervals are their own kind of measure.

Most people's birthdays are unremarkable slots in the calendar. Yours requires the calendar to do something it only does sixteen times in a century. That seems about right for someone born on the day Agadir was destroyed and rebuilt, in the year of the Gerboise Bleue and the Squaw Valley Olympics and the sixteen nations finding independence — into a world that couldn't sit still long enough to be ordinary.
